title: Tanker Mined in Hormuz and Houthi Missiles Hit Saudi Refineries, Even After Iran and Riyadh Agreed to Talk
subhead: Mines in the Strait of Hormuz and a six-target Houthi salvo on Saudi oil and airport infrastructure undercut this week's Tehran diplomacy, while Washington's last diplomatic overture to Iran runs on a seven-day clock that starts only if Tehran freezes its nuclear programme first.

sections.heading: Hormuz: mines, burning tankers and a strait nobody can reopen
sections.body:
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said three tankers caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after striking naval mines, and that a fourth vessel hit mines in the eastern part of the waterway, according to Al Jazeera's live coverage on Friday. There has been no independent confirmation of the number of vessels damaged or of their cargoes; what is verified is that the IRGC itself is now publicly describing the strait as mined.

The practical effect is that shipping insurers, tanker owners and Gulf states get a fresh signal that the waterway remains unsafe regardless of what is agreed in negotiations. Any deal that reopens Hormuz has to survive an active mine threat — laying and clearing mines takes days or weeks, and is a decision Iran can reverse unilaterally.

The diplomatic track is a letter. The Guardian reported Thursday that US Vice President JD Vance wrote to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, on Sunday after mainly Qatari mediation. Under the proposal Tehran would make commitments on its nuclear programme up front, and Hormuz would reopen within seven days in return for US sanctions relief. Rezaei and parliamentary speaker Mohammad Ghalibaf met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei last week to discuss the risk of a new war.

Tehran is resisting front-loaded, irreversible concessions. Ghalibaf wrote on X that 'the carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran' and that progress requires its seven conditions to be agreed first — lifting sanctions, ending asset freezes and ending the war on all fronts, which in practice means an Israeli ceasefire in Lebanon. Iran has floated blending down its highly enriched uranium stockpile rather than exporting it, and is reluctant to readmit UN inspectors. Senator Chris Murphy, briefed on the military options, called the war plan 'insane'. A US attack would follow Tuesday's midterms if diplomacy fails, and a caretaker Israeli government would be its likely partner.

Sources: Al Jazeera live blog (30 Oct); The Guardian (29 Oct), citing Qatari mediation and Murphy's remarks at the Middle East Institute.
sections.whyItMatters: A mined Hormuz plus a proposal that hinges on Iran giving up its nuclear leverage before anything is eased are the two poles of this crisis. Nothing that has happened this week moves them closer together.

sections.heading: Houthis strike Ras Tanura and Riyadh's airport days after Iran-Saudi talks
sections.body:
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement on X that the group carried out six operations: a ballistic missile at the Ras Tanura refinery, a missile at an Aramco facility in Abqaiq, multiple missiles at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, a drone at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, a ballistic missile at the Rabigh refinery, and an attack on a Saudi military headquarters in Najran.

There has been no Saudi confirmation and no independent corroboration of the claims — that caveat matters, because the Houthis have an interest in inflating the reach of their arsenal. But the target list itself is the story: two refineries, two international airports and a military command node inside a single salvo, spanning the kingdom from the eastern oil belt to Riyadh and the southern border.

The timing is what makes it significant. Al Jazeera notes the attacks came despite a rare meeting of senior Saudi and Iranian officials in Tehran earlier this week, attended by high-level representatives from Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, after which the two sides agreed to resolve regional differences through dialogue. The Houthis either cannot be restrained by Tehran or are being used as the lever that keeps pressure on Riyadh while Iran negotiates.

Sources: Al Jazeera (30 Oct), quoting Saree's statement and reporting the absence of Saudi confirmation; Al Jazeera's Iran war live blog.
sections.whyItMatters: If Iran cannot or will not stop Houthi strikes during its own diplomatic opening, Riyadh's incentive to bankroll a US-Iran deal weakens sharply. Saudi consent is what makes a Gulf-wide escalation tolerable for Washington.

sections.heading: Dnipro strike kills 14 as a US-brokered truce holds in Kherson
sections.body:
A Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in Dnipro on Thursday, killing at least 14 people and wounding at least 14 others, including an 11-year-old boy, according to Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha via the BBC. Ukrzaliznytsia, the state railway operator, said a passenger train bound for Zaporizhzhia was at the platform when the drone struck. Mayor Borys Filatov said a drone hit an electric civilian train; Russia's military has not commented.

President Volodymyr Zelensky described the strike as an attack on a platform where a commuter and a passenger train were standing, and called for further US, European and G7 sanctions on Russia — repeating his criticism of the deal struck earlier this month between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin that eased some sanctions on Moscow.

Two hundred kilometres west, Kherson has had its first two days of quiet in nearly five years. A US-brokered temporary ceasefire, the result of efforts by First Lady Melania Trump to arrange safe passage out of the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky across the Dnipro, runs until Sunday. Russia has been clearing mines from the road ahead of a planned civilian evacuation on Friday. Ukrainian officials and residents fear Moscow is using the lull to reinforce for a renewed push on Kherson next week.

Sources: BBC News (29 Oct) reporting Hanzha, Filatov and Zelensky; BBC News (30 Oct) on the Kherson truce and Oleshky evacuation.
sections.whyItMatters: The same week Washington eased sanctions on Moscow, a Russian drone killed 14 civilians at a Ukrainian station. That contradiction is now the central political problem for Kyiv's supporters — and a humanitarian truce that may double as a Russian resupply window gives them little to show for it.

sections.heading: The EU offers Canada a status that does not yet exist
sections.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told the two-day Canada-EU summit in Montreal on Thursday that 'associate membership' would be 'a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before', open only to the closest partners outside Europe and covering alignment on governance and policy plus research and innovation cooperation, the BBC reported.

The status does not currently exist in EU law. Von der Leyen first floated it last month after Canadian Prime Minister Carney told the European Parliament that Canada and Europe were 'stronger together' in the face of 'geopolitical rupture'. Not every member state is on board: Germany and others are reportedly questioning the label, worried about giving Canada preferential treatment over other candidates.

For all the ambiguity, the direction is notable. Brussels is trying to build a tier of privileged non-European partners without offering accession — a template that would apply to other middle powers if it works.

Sources: BBC News (29 Oct), quoting von der Leyen's Montreal remarks and reporting German reservations.
sections.whyItMatters: A new membership category designed for one country is a small institutional change with a large precedent: it gives the EU a way to bind democratic middle powers closer without treaty change or enlargement votes.

sections.heading: Washington sanctions Rwanda's defence ministry over M23
sections.body:
The US Treasury sanctioned Rwanda's defence ministry and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a bank serving Rwandan security services, over support for the M23 rebellion in eastern DR Congo, the BBC reported. Treasury alleges the ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 with weapons, equipment, logistics and training, and that the bank handled tens of millions of dollars in transactions for M23 and its political wing, the Congo River Alliance, helped pay for military equipment for Rwandan forces from China and moved gold from rebel-held areas to Kigali.

The sanctions are meant to reinforce the Washington Accords, signed by the Congolese and Rwandan presidents in December 2025 under US mediation, which have not stopped the fighting that began when M23 seized Goma and Bukavu in early 2025. Rwandan government spokesperson Yolande Makolo told the BBC that Kigali remains ready to implement the accords but that the DRC has not neutralised the FDLR militia. Kinshasa's foreign ministry welcomed the sanctions.

Washington is also targeting the mineral chain directly. M23 holds gold sites in South Kivu and Rubaya, a major coltan area in North Kivu, and Treasury alleges Rwanda exports more minerals than it produces.

Sources: BBC News (29 Oct), citing US Treasury designation and statements from Makolo and the DRC foreign ministry.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first time Washington has sanctioned a Rwandan government ministry rather than individuals, and it cuts at the bank that pays Kigali's soldiers. It tests whether a US-brokered deal can be enforced on its own signatory — and whether coltan supply chains react.

sections.heading: The rest of the board: China's purges, Lagarde's exit, a $3bn exchange freeze
sections.body:
China's fifth plenum expelled a record 33 Central Committee members, 16 of them from the military, and attendance fell below 300 for the first time in Xi Jinping's 14 years of leadership — 279 members against 315 a year earlier, per the BBC. The expelled include former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui and ex-generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Carnegie China's Chong Ja Ian told the BBC the campaign has become 'an effort to consolidate and maintain authority'. Total removals under Xi's third term now stand at 51, against 35 and five in the previous two.

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said she will step down in March, nine months early, to gain the 'freedom of speech' to engage on non-monetary matters, speaking after the ECB held its deposit rate at 2.5% with inflation at 3.8%, the highest since September 2023, per The Guardian. She is tipped as a candidate to run the World Economic Forum.

Binance said roughly $3bn in funds were frozen after what it called a 'potential security issue', suspending deposits and withdrawals as a precaution and saying it would cover all losses. Founder Changpeng Zhao said on X it 'does look like a hack'; Bitcoin fell about 5% below $77,000. If confirmed, Al Jazeera notes it would exceed the $1.5bn Lazarus Group heist of 2025 as the largest crypto theft on record.

Sources: BBC News (29 Oct); The Guardian (29 Oct); Al Jazeera (30 Oct).
sections.whyItMatters: Three unrelated but telling data points: the largest purge cycle of Xi's tenure hitting the military hardest, the eurozone's chief central banker leaving to speak politically, and the world's biggest crypto venue freezing billions — all in 48 hours.

bottomLine: Iran is publicly describing the Strait of Hormuz as mined while a Qatari-brokered Vance letter asks it to freeze its nuclear programme before the strait reopens — an offer Tehran has so far refused to sequence the way Washington wants — and the Houthis marked the week of Iran-Saudi talks by claiming strikes on Ras Tanura, Abqaiq, Rabigh and two Saudi international airports. Washington's post-midterm choice for Iran therefore rests on a reply that has not arrived, a strait that cannot be cleared overnight, and a Gulf partner that is being hit while it negotiates. Elsewhere the pattern is pressure applied unevenly: a Russian drone kills 14 in Dnipro in the same week Washington eased sanctions on Moscow, while a US-brokered truce keeps Kherson quiet until Sunday and possibly gives Russia time to resupply for what comes after.
